hookLine: Two judges were paid to send children to jail.

captions.text: In 2007, a seventeen-year-old girl in Pennsylvania built
a fake web page that made fun of her assistant
principal.
It was a prank.
She expected, at worst, detention.
A judge sent her away for three months.
The hearing lasted about ninety seconds —
and no one in that room told
her she was allowed a lawyer.
The rest, she would not learn for years:
that the judge who signed her order was being paid
by the jail that took her in.
Paid for every child he sent through its doors.
Luzerne County, Pennsylvania.
Coal country, long after the coal.
In the city of Wilkes-Barre stood a courthouse
that was supposed to be the one place a kid
who went wrong could be set right.
The children who passed through it had done small things.
A shoving match in a hallway.
Twenty dollars of stolen makeup.
A rude page online.
The kind of thing that,
almost anywhere else, ends with a warning and a ride
home.
Here it began with a signature.
A child was handed a form giving up the right
to a lawyer —
and it was handed over the way you'd pass someone
a receipt, as if it were nothing.
No one explained what it meant.
And so the children,
young and scared and taught to trust the adults
in the room, signed away the one protection
that might have saved them.
Then came a man in a robe named Mark Ciavarella.
Half of the children who signed that form left
his courtroom in handcuffs,
bound for a locked facility.
In the rest of the state,
that number was eight in a hundred.
And placement was not a slap on the wrist.
It meant being taken that same day —
cuffed, photographed, driven hours from home,
and left to sleep behind a locked door for weeks
or months.
Missing school.
Missing a parent's face.
Learning to think of yourself as an inmate
before you were old enough to drive.
It was fast, too.
A minute. Two.
A boy could be named a delinquent and led
out a side door before his mother rose
from her seat.
Some parents drove home and only understood,
hours later, that they would not be tucking their child
in that night —
or for many nights after.
There were no long deliberations,
no weighing of the evidence.
There was a decision that seemed to have been made
before anyone walked in.
And still the parents believed it was justice,
because who doesn't believe a judge?
That belief —
that a courtroom is a safe place to bring
your child —
was the first thing being sold.
To see what was really happening,
follow the money.
It starts one floor up.
There were two judges.
Ciavarella, in the juvenile court.
And Michael Conahan, the president judge —
the one who held the county's checkbook.
The county ran its own juvenile detention center,
paid for with tax dollars.
Conahan starved it of funding and moved it toward
the door.
He went further:
he put his name to an agreement that guaranteed
a steady stream of children to a brand-new,
private, for-profit jail.
A guarantee.
In writing.
That a certain number of kids would be needed.
A for-profit jail lives by one number.
Empty beds cost money;
full beds make it.
And now someone had promised the beds would be full.
They were filled the only way they could be —
one child at a time,
by the judge down the hall.
A developer named Robert Mericle built those facilities.
An attorney named Robert Powell owned and ran them.
Across roughly three years,
the two men passed about two point eight million dollars
to the judges.
It didn't move in open daylight;
it moved through side accounts and quiet transfers,
dressed up as a "finder's fee." A referral.
Money, they said, for helping the places get built
and kept busy.
Take the language away and it is very simple.
A child walked in.
A judge sent that child to a cell.
A payment followed.
And the children who came without a lawyer?
In that courtroom they appeared seven to eleven times more
often than anywhere else in the state —
because a child with no lawyer is a child
who cannot fight back.
Every hearing that felt too quick was not impatience
on the bench.
It was inventory.
And it did not happen once.
It happened morning after morning,
for years, until the children who had been fed
into those private beds numbered in the thousands.
No one pulled the alarm,
because on paper each of those hearings looked perfectly
legal —
a judge, a courtroom,
a signature.
The machine hid inside the shape of ordinary justice.
A number this size goes silent.
So stand in one house.
Ed Kenzakoski was seventeen.
A wrestler, with a father who had a future picked
out for him.
He came before Ciavarella on a small charge,
and he was sent away.
The boy who came home was not the boy
who left.
He carried it for years —
the record, the lost time,
the verdict passed on him at seventeen
that he could never quite outrun.
He struggled.
He tried to hold a life together and couldn't.
At twenty-three, he took his own life.
His mother is Sandy Fonzo.
And when Ciavarella walked down the steps of a federal
courthouse years later —
a defendant now, out on bail,
calm in a dark suit —
she was there.
She met him on the pavement in front
of the cameras, grief turned to fury,
and demanded to know how the man who had broken
her son could stand there and say he'd done nothing
wrong.
He fixed his tie and looked past her.
He had nothing.
There is nothing to say.
Now set that against the size of it.
Thousands of children told,
at thirteen, at fifteen,
that they were criminals —
and, being children, believing it.
Some came out and never found their footing.
A record that trailed them onto every job form
and every college application,
quietly closing doors they never saw close.
Years later, grown now,
some of them would sit in front of cameras
and try to explain what it does to a person
to be sold at fifteen.
Some still can't.
That is the part no ruling returns and no settlement
buys back.
For years it held —
because of who was doing the complaining.
A kid with a record.
A parent who "should have raised them better." Easy voices
to wave off.
And they were waved off,
again and again.
Then one more mother picked up the phone —
and called a small nonprofit in Philadelphia,
the Juvenile Law Center.
Its lawyers pulled the files expecting a few heavy-handed
sentences.
They found a machine:
hundreds of children, the same pattern each time —
minutes in the room,
no lawyer, straight to the same private beds.
At the same time,
federal investigators were quietly building their own case,
following the money the judges thought no one could see.
And it might all have stayed buried —
a local story, a few angry parents easy to ignore —
if the families had not refused to go quiet,
and if, later, a documentary had not put their faces
on a screen and made the rest of the country
finally look.
For the first time,
the children in those files stopped being case numbers.
They were somebody's kid.
They had names.
The Juvenile Law Center took it to the Pennsylvania Supreme
Court, and the court did a rare thing.
It reached back into Ciavarella's courtroom and unmade it —
throwing out thousands of adjudications,
clearing the records of as many as several thousand
children.
The state, in plain terms,
admitting that none of it should ever have counted.
But a cleared record is not a returned childhood.
Behind each of those cases was a year,
or two, or three,
that the county had already spent —
nights in a cell that no order could give back.
The paperwork could be erased.
The time could not.
Then the law turned on the men who had sold
it.
Michael Conahan pleaded guilty to racketeering;
seventeen and a half years.
Ciavarella refused to fold —
he insisted the money was a legal finder's fee,
not a bribe, that he had never sentenced a child
for cash.
A jury heard him out and convicted him anyway,
on racketeering and corruption,
and he was given twenty-eight years.
Later, a court ordered the two of them to pay
more than two hundred million dollars to the families
they had harmed.
It was, at last,
a kind of justice —
and it forced a change:
Pennsylvania moved to make sure a child standing
in a courtroom actually has a lawyer at their side.
But ask Sandy Fonzo if it was enough.
We like to believe a courtroom is the one room
where the money stays outside the door.
That the people with power are held to a higher
line than the rest of us.
For thousands of children in one American county,
that line had a price.
It worked out to a few thousand dollars a head.
The judges are named and gone.
One spent years in prison.
The other, quietly, was granted an early release and walked
back out into the world while the children he sentenced
were still carrying theirs.
Because that is the last,
hardest truth of this story:
the men could be punished,
and still the years don't come back.
If this is a story that should be seen
and not buried, subscribe —
the next one opens the way this one did:
an ordinary person, and a system that was never meant
to reach them.
Because the distance between a family like yours
and a family like theirs is far shorter
than we let ourselves believe.
